disease.name: Fistula
disease.scientific_name: Fistula-in-Ano / Anal Fistula / Perianal Fistula / Anorectal Fistula
disease.icd_10_code: K60.3 (Anal fistula); K60.4 (Rectal fistula); K60.5 (Anorectal fistula); K57.2 (Diverticular disease with fistula); K50.8 (Crohn's disease with fistula); K63.2 (Fistula of intestine); N82 (Fistulae involving female genital tract); K63.3 (Ulcer of intestine); N32.1 (Vesicointestinal fistula)
disease.category: Colorectal / Proctological / Anorectal Disease / Surgical Condition

overview.description: A fistula is an abnormal, epithelium-lined tract or tunnel forming an unnatural connection between two body surfaces — either between two hollow organs, or between an organ and the skin. In clinical practice, the most common and surgically significant fistula is the anal fistula (fistula-in-ano) — an abnormal tract connecting the anal canal (typically at the level of the dentate line, where anal glands open) to the perianal skin surface, with a characteristically intermittently or persistently discharging external opening. The vast majority (90%) of anal fistulae arise from infected anal glands — the cryptoglandular origin — which cause an anorectal abscess that either spontaneously drains through the perianal skin or is surgically drained, leaving behind a persistently infected epithelialised tract. Fistulae represent one of the most technically challenging conditions in colorectal surgery — because the tract often passes through or around the anal sphincter muscles, and treatment must eliminate the fistula without causing faecal incontinence, which would be as disabling as the fistula itself.
overview.affected_organ: Anal canal and perianal tissues; internal and external anal sphincters; ischiorectal/ischioanal fossae; intersphincteric space; levator ani musculature (in high fistulae)
overview.prevalence: Anal fistula affects approximately 1-2 per 10,000 adults per year. Male to female ratio approximately 2:1 for simple cryptoglandular fistulae. In patients with Crohn's disease: cumulative incidence of perianal fistula is 20-40% over 20 years. In India: anal fistula is among the most common anorectal conditions presenting to surgical outpatient departments.
overview.age_group: Peak in adults aged 30-50 years (cryptoglandular); Crohn's fistulae can present at any age from young adulthood
overview.sex_ratio: Men 2:1 over women for simple cryptoglandular fistulae (possibly related to more deeply located male anal glands); women more often affected by rectovaginal fistulae and obstetric anorectal injury
overview.chronic_note: Fistulae rarely heal spontaneously and almost invariably require surgical or interventional treatment; Crohn's fistulae require long-term medical and surgical management
overview.key_fact: The cardinal surgical principle of anal fistula treatment: 'Cut through as little sphincter as possible while achieving lasting fistula closure.' Every millimetre of additional sphincter division increases incontinence risk — making sphincter-sparing procedures the priority for complex and high fistulae.

fistula_anatomy_and_classification.cryptoglandular_theory: The most widely accepted aetiology of anal fistula — proposed by Parks, Gordon, and Hardcastle in 1976. The anal canal contains 6-8 anal glands (crypts of Morgagni) at the level of the dentate line in the intersphincteric space. These glands normally secrete mucus. When an anal gland becomes obstructed and infected, an intersphincteric abscess forms. This abscess may track in various directions: downward to the anal verge (perianal abscess); through the external sphincter to the ischiorectal fossa (ischiorectal/ischioanal abscess); upward above the levator ani (supralevator abscess). When the abscess spontaneously drains or is surgically incised, the infected track may remain patent as a fistula tract — because the internal opening (at the anal gland in the dentate line) continues to act as a source of infection.

parks_classification.intersphincteric: Most common (45-70%); tract passes through the intersphincteric plane to the perianal skin; LOW risk to sphincter; LOW incontinence risk after treatment
parks_classification.transsphincteric: 30-40% of cases; tract passes through both the internal and external anal sphincters to the ischiorectal fossa and perianal skin; MODERATE sphincter involvement; treatment requires careful sphincter management
parks_classification.suprasphincteric: 5% of cases; tract goes upward from intersphincteric plane over the puborectalis muscle and down through levator ani to ischiorectal fossa; HIGH sphincter involvement; complex management
parks_classification.extrasphincteric: 1-2%; tract passes from perineal skin through the levator ani directly into the rectum, bypassing both sphincters; usually secondary to Crohn's disease, pelvic sepsis, trauma, or iatrogenic injury; VERY complex management

simple_vs_complex.simple: Low intersphincteric or low transsphincteric fistula; single tract; no active anorectal disease; not associated with Crohn's; not in field of previous radiation; not associated with local malignancy; no incontinence pre-operatively; no circumferential component
simple_vs_complex.complex: High transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, or extrasphincteric; multiple tracts or horseshoe extension; previous sphincter injury; associated Crohn's disease; rectovaginal fistula; recurrent after previous repair; active proctitis or mucosal disease; high incontinence risk

goodsalls_rule.description: A useful clinical guide predicting the course of the fistula internal opening based on the location of the external opening
goodsalls_rule.posterior_external_opening: External openings POSTERIOR to a transverse line through the anus (behind the anal opening): the internal opening is at the POSTERIOR MIDLINE (6 o'clock); the fistula tract runs in a curved path to the posterior midline
goodsalls_rule.anterior_external_opening: External openings ANTERIOR to the transverse line: the internal opening is at the nearest anal crypt (directly radial); the tract runs in a straight line
goodsalls_rule.exception: If the external opening is more than 3cm from the anal verge, regardless of position, the internal opening is likely to be at the posterior midline
goodsalls_rule.limitation: Goodsall's rule is a rough guide with significant exceptions, particularly in Crohn's fistulae and horseshoe fistulae; MRI has superseded Goodsall's rule for surgical planning

types.name: Simple Intersphincteric Anal Fistula
types.description: The most common type — the fistula tract passes entirely through the intersphincteric plane (between the internal and external anal sphincters) from the internal opening at the dentate line to an external opening on the perianal skin. The external sphincter is NOT crossed — making this a 'low' fistula with minimal incontinence risk after treatment.
types.sphincter_involvement: Internal sphincter only — external sphincter is preserved
types.treatment: Fistulotomy (laying open) — safe; excellent cure rates; very low incontinence risk

types.name: Transsphincteric Anal Fistula
types.description: The fistula tract passes through both the internal AND external anal sphincters before reaching the ischiorectal fossa and external skin. The amount of external sphincter involved determines treatment approach: low transsphincteric (crossing the lower portion of the EAS — can often be laid open safely); high transsphincteric (crossing a significant proportion of the EAS — laying open risks incontinence — requires sphincter-sparing approach).
types.sphincter_involvement: Both IAS and EAS — portion of EAS crossed determines risk
types.treatment_low: Low (involves <30% EAS): fistulotomy may be considered; seton may be used
types.treatment_high: High (involves >30% EAS): seton, LIFT procedure, advancement flap, VAAFT, fibrin glue — sphincter-sparing approaches

types.name: Suprasphincteric Anal Fistula
types.description: A high and complex fistula — the tract passes upward from the intersphincteric plane over (above) the puborectalis muscle, then curves downward through the levator ani muscle into the ischiorectal fossa and out to the perianal skin. The entire external sphincter and levator ani are crossed — making fistulotomy impossible without complete incontinence. Sphincter-preserving surgery is mandatory.
types.treatment: Staged seton; advancement flap; LIFT; VAAFT; multiple procedures often required
types.prognosis: Challenging — recurrence rates higher than lower fistulae

types.name: Extrasphincteric Anal Fistula
types.description: The rarest and most complex type — the fistula passes from the perianal skin directly through the levator ani muscle into the rectum, entirely bypassing the sphincter complex. Usually NOT of cryptoglandular origin — typically secondary to Crohn's disease, pelvic sepsis from appendicitis or diverticular disease, penetrating pelvic trauma, or iatrogenic injury from instrumentation or surgery.
types.causes: Crohn's disease; pelvic sepsis (diverticular, appendix); trauma; post-radiation; iatrogenic
types.treatment: Usually requires staged approaches; treat underlying cause (Crohn's — biological therapy); defunctioning stoma (temporary colostomy) to allow healing; complex reconstructive procedures; rarely permanent stoma

types.name: Horseshoe Fistula
types.description: A bilateral fistula with a deep postanal space component — the tract passes from the internal opening in the posterior midline around both sides of the anal canal (like a horseshoe) to bilateral external openings on both sides of the anus. The deep postanal space (between the anococcygeal ligament and the external sphincter) is the primary abscess cavity. Complex to treat — requires unroofing of the deep postanal space (Hanley procedure) and staged seton to the two lateral limbs.
types.anatomy: Deep postanal space is the origin; bilateral extensions to ischiorectal fossae via the transsphincteric route
types.treatment: Modified Hanley procedure; staged approaches; technically demanding

types.name: Crohn's Perianal Fistula
types.description: Perianal fistulae associated with Crohn's disease are a distinct and particularly challenging entity — more complex, more likely to be multiple, more likely to be associated with proctitis, skin tags, and abscesses, more likely to recur after treatment, and requiring combined medical and surgical management. Perianal disease (fistulae, skin tags, abscesses, fissures) affects 20-40% of Crohn's patients over 20 years. Crohn's fistulae may be low or complex, and crucially, may be associated with active rectal inflammation (proctitis) that impairs healing and contraindicates sphincterotomy.
types.prevalence: 20-40% of Crohn's patients develop perianal fistulae
types.characteristics: May be multiple; large; deep; associated perianal skin disease; often minimally symptomatic despite complexity; recurrent; associated active proctitis
types.treatment: Biological therapy (infliximab, adalimumab) is the cornerstone; seton drainage; LIFT; stem cell therapy (Alofisel); defunctioning stoma for severe cases; avoiding fistulotomy in active proctitis
types.van_assche_score: MRI-based scoring system for Crohn's fistula complexity and treatment response: assesses number of tracts, extensions, hyperintensity (inflammation), rectal wall involvement

types.name: Rectovaginal Fistula
types.description: An abnormal communication between the rectum (or anal canal) and the vagina — allowing passage of faeces or gas into the vagina. Causes: obstetric injury (most common — 3rd/4th degree perineal tears); Crohn's disease; radiation (post-pelvic radiotherapy for cervical, rectal, or prostate cancer); surgical trauma; carcinoma; diverticular disease. Classified by level: low (below dentate line — anovaginal); mid (between dentate line and cervix); high (at or above cervix).
types.prevalence: Most common in post-partum women and Crohn's disease
types.symptoms: Passage of faeces or gas per vagina; vaginitis; malodorous vaginal discharge; recurrent urinary tract infections
types.diagnosis: Clinical inspection; methylene blue test (dye instilled per rectum — if detected in vagina confirms connection); MRI pelvis; EUA
types.treatment: Low anovaginal fistula: perineal repair; advancement flap. Mid fistula (obstetric): muscle interposition (Martius flap); transabdominal repair. Crohn's fistula: medical (biologic) + seton + eventual definitive repair after quiescence

types.name: Enterocutaneous Fistula
types.description: An abnormal communication between the intestine (small or large bowel) and the skin. Most commonly occur post-surgically (anastomotic leak after bowel surgery — 75-80% of cases) or from Crohn's disease, diverticular disease, radiation injury, trauma, or malignancy. High-output fistulae (>500mL/day — small bowel origin) have significant metabolic consequences: dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, malnutrition, and skin excoriation. Low-output fistulae (<200mL/day — colonic origin) are less metabolically challenging but prone to infection.
types.spontaneous_closure_factors: FRIENDS mnemonic (factors preventing spontaneous closure): Foreign body; Radiation; Inflammation/Infection; Epithelialisation; Neoplasia; Distal obstruction; Short tract (<2cm)
types.management: SNAP principles: Sepsis control; Nutrition (TPN or enteral); Anatomy (fistulogram/CT); Protection of skin (stoma bags); Definitive procedure when patient optimised

severity_levels.name: Simple / Low Fistula
severity_levels.description: Low intersphincteric or low transsphincteric fistula; single tract; minimal sphincter involvement
severity_levels.symptoms: Persistent perianal discharge (intermittent); mild perianal discomfort; palpable external opening on perianal skin
severity_levels.mri_finding: Single simple tract; no extensions; no horseshoe component; no collections
severity_levels.management: Fistulotomy (laying open) — day case surgery; >95% cure; minimal incontinence risk

severity_levels.name: Moderate / Complex Fistula
severity_levels.description: High transsphincteric fistula or multiple tracts; significant sphincter involvement; or simple fistula with specific complexity factors
severity_levels.symptoms: Persistent discharge; perianal pain; possible acute episodes of perianal abscess; pruritis; faecal soiling around external opening
severity_levels.associated_disease: May be Crohn's-associated; may have failed previous treatment
severity_levels.mri_finding: High transsphincteric tract; secondary extensions; T2 hyperintensity (inflammation); possible horseshoe component
severity_levels.management: Staged approach: draining seton first; then LIFT/advancement flap/VAAFT; multiple procedures may be required
severity_levels.continence_risk: Moderate (10-20% incontinence without careful sphincter-sparing approach)

severity_levels.name: Severe / Highly Complex Fistula
severity_levels.description: Suprasphincteric or extrasphincteric fistula; Crohn's fistula with proctitis; multiple complex tracts; horseshoe with both limbs; rectovaginal fistula; recurrent after multiple failed repairs
severity_levels.sphincter_risk: High (>70% sphincter involvement) or involvement of levator ani/supralevator structures
severity_levels.symptoms: Significant discharge; pain; incontinence (gas, occasionally liquid); failed previous surgeries; quality of life severely impaired
severity_levels.associated_disease: Crohn's disease (often); active proctitis; radiation history; pelvic malignancy
severity_levels.mri_finding: Complex multi-branching tracts; supralevator extensions; horseshoe; active inflammation; possible associated cavity/collections
severity_levels.management: Long-term draining seton; biologic therapy (if Crohn's); stem cell therapy; defunctioning stoma; multidisciplinary team (MDT); liver/colorectal surgeon + gastroenterologist + IBD nurse + stoma therapist
severity_levels.continence_risk: High; permanent defunctioning stoma may ultimately be the best quality-of-life option in some patients

primary_cause_cryptoglandular.mechanism: The cryptoglandular theory (Parks 1961): Anal glands in the intersphincteric space become occluded → infection → intersphincteric abscess → spreads to adjacent spaces → drains spontaneously or surgically through skin → epithelialised track persists as fistula tract between the infected anal gland (internal opening) and external drainage point (external opening)
primary_cause_cryptoglandular.incidence: ~90% of anal fistulae arise from this mechanism
primary_cause_cryptoglandular.progression: Perianal abscess → fistula develops in approximately 30-50% of adequately drained anorectal abscesses

specific_causes.detail: Approximately 30-50% of drained perianal abscesses result in a subsequent anal fistula. Fistula formation is more likely when: the abscess is recurrent; primary drainage is incomplete; the internal opening (anal gland source) was not identified and addressed at drainage. Incision and drainage alone treats the acute abscess but does NOT eliminate the fistula tract.
specific_causes.prevention: Identification of the internal opening at time of abscess drainage (where possible) and primary fistulotomy (in low intersphincteric fistula at drainage EUA) may reduce fistula formation rate

specific_causes.detail: The most important secondary cause — Crohn's-associated perianal fistulae affect 20-40% of patients over the disease course. Crohn's fistulae arise from transmural intestinal inflammation extending into perianal tissues, from deep anorectal ulcers, or from fistulising disease specifically. Crohn's perianal fistulae are often complex, multiple, and refractory to standard surgical treatment — requiring biological therapy (anti-TNF) as the cornerstone of management.

An important cause in India and other high-TB burden countries. Intestinal TB can cause bowel fistulae (enterocutaneous, enterovaginal). Perianal TB causes: multiple chronic perianal fistulae that are indolent, pale, and less painful than cryptoglandular fistulae; biopsy shows caseating granulomas and AFB on ZN stain. Must be considered in all patients with multiple or unusual perianal fistulae in India. Treatment: standard anti-TB therapy (DOTS regime) + surgery after culture-confirmed TB is controlled.
specific_causes.india_significance: TB fistulae are significantly more common in India than in high-income countries; maintain a high index of suspicion in all complex perianal fistulae; send biopsies routinely

specific_causes.detail: Pelvic radiotherapy for rectal cancer, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, or uterine cancer causes radiation-induced endarteritis → tissue ischaemia → chronic non-healing ulcers → fistula formation. Radiation fistulae are characterised by: poor healing capacity (ischaemic irradiated tissue); risk of enterovaginal, rectovaginal, colovaginal, or enterocutaneous fistula; very difficult to treat surgically due to poor blood supply. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is an adjunctive treatment for radiation tissue injury.

The most common cause of enterocutaneous fistula — anastomotic leak following bowel resection and anastomosis (colorectal cancer surgery, diverticular disease surgery, IBD surgery) can lead to enteric contents leaking into the peritoneum or through a drain site, establishing a fistula tract. Risk factors for anastomotic leak: left-sided colonic anastomosis; lack of defunctioning stoma; bowel preparation problems; malnutrition; immunosuppression; corticosteroids.
specific_causes.management: SNAP protocol: control sepsis; optimise nutrition (TPN/enteral); define anatomy (CT fistulogram); protect skin (ostomy appliance); plan definitive repair

specific_causes.detail: Complicated diverticular disease can cause colovesical fistula (most common diverticular fistula — between sigmoid colon and bladder; causes pneumaturia — air bubbles in urine, and fecaluria — faeces in urine; predominantly men — women's uterus protects the bladder); colovaginal fistula (after hysterectomy — when uterus no longer separates colon from vagina); colocutaneous fistula; ileosigmoid fistula.
specific_causes.most_common_diverticular_fistula: Colovesical (colovaginal in women with prior hysterectomy) — treated surgically with one-stage resection and anastomosis

specific_causes.detail: Advanced colorectal cancer, anal cancer, cervical cancer, or bladder cancer can invade adjacent structures creating fistulae (rectovaginal, colovesical, enterovesical). Any 'fistula' in a patient with known or suspected malignancy must have the tract biopsied to exclude cancer-related fistula. Non-healing fistulae in patients >50 years should prompt cancer workup.
specific_causes.note: Long-standing chronic Crohn's perianal fistulae carry a small but real risk of squamous cell carcinoma development — any change in a chronic fistula character (increased bleeding, ulceration, pain change) should prompt biopsy

specific_causes.detail: The most common cause of rectovaginal fistula in the world — unrepaired or inadequately repaired 4th degree perineal tears (involving rectum) during vaginal delivery. Also: episiotomy extensions involving rectum; difficult instrumental deliveries. Post-partum rectovaginal fistulae typically present 1-3 months after delivery with passage of flatus or stool vaginally.
specific_causes.grading: 4th degree perineal tear = external sphincter + internal sphincter + rectal mucosa involvement; immediate repair required; fistula complication if repair breaks down

specific_causes.detail: HIV-positive patients, particularly those with low CD4 counts, are at higher risk of complex perianal fistulae — from: opportunistic infections (CMV, Cryptosporidium causing proctitis); higher prevalence of anal HPV infection and condylomata; secondary infections with unusual organisms; impaired healing. ART (antiretroviral therapy) optimisation is the primary adjunct to surgical treatment in HIV-positive patients with fistulae.

risk_factors: Prior anorectal abscess (most important risk factor for fistula development)
Diabetes mellitus (impaired wound healing; higher abscess risk)
Smoking (impaired wound healing; associated with Crohn's activity)

symptoms.cardinal_symptom: The hallmark of anal fistula is PERSISTENT OR RECURRENT PERIANAL DISCHARGE from an external opening on the perianal skin. Unlike abscess (which discharges once then the pain resolves), a fistula continues to discharge intermittently or continuously — because the internal opening from the anal gland source continues to supply infected material to the tract.

primary_symptoms.name: Persistent Perianal Discharge
primary_symptoms.description: The MOST COMMON presenting symptom — the external opening of the fistula chronically discharges serous, seropurulent, or purulent fluid onto the perianal skin. Patients notice: staining of underwear with brown or yellow-green fluid; need to wear a pad at all times; perianal moisture and irritation; sometimes small pieces of faecal material in the discharge. The discharge may be intermittent — particularly when the external opening partially closes, causing accumulation and then re-rupture — with cycling of apparent resolution and re-drainage associated with acute abscess formation.
primary_symptoms.character: Serous (clear); seropurulent (cloudy); purulent (pus); occasionally faecal-stained (in complex fistulae communicating with rectum)
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Moderate — chronic; impairs quality of life

primary_symptoms.name: Perianal Pain and Discomfort
primary_symptoms.description: A constant dull perianal ache or discomfort — distinct from the severe episodic pain of anal fissure. Pain in fistula is from: active inflammatory activity in the tract; partial blockage of the external opening causing accumulation and tension (mini-abscess); associated sphincter spasm. Pain dramatically WORSENS when the external opening blocks (acute abscess-on-fistula) and IMPROVES when the opening drains freely. Severe, throbbing pain in a patient with a known fistula suggests a recurrent abscess requiring urgent drainage.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (patent draining fistula) to Severe (blocked — acute abscess)
primary_symptoms.pattern: Worsens with blockage; improves with drainage

primary_symptoms.name: Palpable External Opening
primary_symptoms.description: The external opening (also called the secondary opening or skin opening) is usually visible and palpable as a small elevated dimple, nodule, or pore on the perianal skin — often within 2-5 cm of the anal verge, surrounding by indurated, reddened or pigmented perianal skin from chronic discharge. May be single or multiple (complex or Crohn's fistulae). Discharge may be expressible from the opening on gentle digital pressure. Hair follicles and granulation tissue may be visible around the external opening.
primary_symptoms.location: Commonly within 2-5cm of the anal verge; position relative to the anal verge guides Goodsall's rule prediction
primary_symptoms.examination: Visible pore or nodule with surrounding fibrosis; gentle palpation expresses discharge

primary_symptoms.name: Recurrent Perianal Abscesses
primary_symptoms.description: Many patients present with a history of RECURRENT PERIANAL ABSCESSES — each time experiencing: sudden onset severe perianal pain; swelling; fever; eventual spontaneous discharge or surgical drainage. This pattern of recurring abscesses from the same region strongly suggests an underlying persistent fistula tract that was not addressed when the initial abscess was drained. Between abscess episodes, patients may have an apparently 'normal' perianal region, or a small persistently discharging sinus.
primary_symptoms.significance: A second anorectal abscess from the same location strongly suggests an underlying fistula — examination for fistula is mandatory
primary_symptoms.pattern: Cyclic: abscess builds (pain, swelling, fever) → drains → temporary relief → recurrence weeks to months later

primary_symptoms.name: Pruritus Ani (Perianal Itching)
primary_symptoms.description: Persistent or intermittent perianal itching from: chronic moisture and discharge maceration of the perianal skin; faecal contamination of the perianal skin from discharge; secondary dermatitis; fungal colonisation of the moist perianal area; skin irritation from continuous discharge.
primary_symptoms.management: Keep the perianal area clean and dry; moisture-wicking pads; barrier creams (zinc oxide); topical antifungal if Candida present

primary_symptoms.name: Passage of Gas or Faeces from External Opening (Complex Fistulae)
primary_symptoms.description: In highly complex fistulae with a direct communication to the anal canal or rectum, patients may occasionally notice: flatus (gas) passing from the external opening on the perianal skin; faecal-stained discharge; or even passage of formed stool from the fistula. This indicates a low-resistance large-calibre fistula tract directly communicating with the anal lumen. Similarly, in rectovaginal fistulae, patients notice passage of gas or faeces per vagina.
primary_symptoms.significance: This symptom indicates complex high-volume fistula — urgent colorectal surgery review required
primary_symptoms.significance_rectovaginal: In women: passage of gas or faeces per vagina = rectovaginal fistula until proved otherwise

secondary_symptoms: Fever and systemic features — in acute abscess-on-fistula phase; temperature >38°C; malaise; rigors if bacteraemia from perianal sepsis
Perianal skin excoriation — chemical dermatitis from chronic discharge; skin breaks down and becomes raw; secondary bacterial or fungal infection; significant discomfort
Blood in discharge — granulation tissue at internal or external opening bleeds on contact; small amounts of blood mixed with discharge are common; heavier bleeding requires assessment
Faecal urgency and soiling — from inflammation close to the sphincter; in complex fistulae, the inflammatory process may reduce functional sphincter capacity
Palpable induration — hardened, fibrous, rope-like cord under the perianal skin connecting external opening to the anal canal — palpable in superficial fistulae on gentle bidigital examination
Multiple external openings — in Crohn's fistulae, horseshoe fistulae, or recurrent complex fistulae — multiple dimples or pores visible on the perianal skin

Depression and psychological burden — chronic discharge, social embarrassment, odour, need to wear pads, recurrent painful abscesses, and repeated surgeries cause significant psychological morbidity — anxiety, depression, sexual dysfunction, social isolation

diagnostic_approach.overview: Anal fistula diagnosis begins with careful clinical history and examination, progresses to imaging (MRI pelvis — gold standard for complex fistulae), and ultimately to definitive anatomical assessment under anaesthesia (EUA — Examination Under Anaesthesia) where the full extent of the fistula can be determined and treatment initiated simultaneously. The key diagnostic objectives are: (1) Confirm fistula diagnosis; (2) Identify the internal opening; (3) Determine Parks' classification (relationship to sphincters); (4) Identify any secondary tracts, extensions, or collections; (5) Exclude secondary causes (Crohn's, TB, malignancy).
diagnostic_approach.three_step_rule: The three anatomical questions before fistula surgery: (1) Where is the primary internal opening? (2) What is the course of the primary tract? (3) Are there secondary tracts or extensions?

medical_history: Duration of discharge and pain; character and volume of discharge
History of prior anorectal abscesses — number, locations, treatment
Previous fistula surgery and procedures — what was done; pathology report
IBD history: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis; GI symptoms (diarrhoea, abdominal pain, blood PR, weight loss)
TB history: prior TB; TB contact; residence in endemic area; BCG vaccination status; TB treatment history
HIV status and risk factors; CD4 count if HIV-positive
Obstetric history: vaginal deliveries; perineal tears; forceps delivery
Pelvic radiotherapy history (prostate, cervical, rectal cancer treatment)
Medications: immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, biologics (important for wound healing assessment)
Continence history: current bowel control (any gas/stool incontinence — critical baseline for consent and surgical planning)
physical_examination: External perianal inspection: number and location of external openings; character of discharge; perianal skin condition (excoriation, maceration, skin tags, condylomata); measure external opening distance from anal verge
Goodsall's rule application: predict likely internal opening location from external opening position
Palpation: palpate for subcutaneous cord (fistula tract) connecting external opening to anal canal; assess induration; multiple tracts possible
Bimanual palpation: using one finger in the anal canal and thumb externally to palpate the fistula tract between the two

Digital rectal examination (DRE): assess internal opening (tender induration at dentate line); sphincter tone; rectal mucosal assessment (exclude proctitis, rectal mass); assess rectal vault for supralevator extension

Proctoscopy: visualise the anal canal; identify internal opening at dentate level (often hyperaemic or granulating); injection of hydrogen peroxide or methylene blue via external opening may identify the internal opening by bubbles or dye appearing at the dentate line

Assessment of continence: ask specifically about pre-existing incontinence to gas, liquid, or solid stool — critical for surgical consent and planning (pre-existing incontinence is a major risk factor for worsened continence after sphincterotomy)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: MRI Pelvis (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) — Gold Standard for Complex Fistulae
diagnostic_tests.description: MRI pelvis is the GOLD STANDARD for mapping complex anal fistulae — providing unparalleled soft tissue resolution of the sphincter complex, fistula tract relationships, extensions, collections, and internal opening. T2-weighted sequences show the fistula tract as a bright (hyperintense) signal within the darker sphincter muscle. Fat-suppressed sequences (STIR or T2 FS) enhance identification of active inflammation and fluid collections. The Van Assche MRI score provides a validated quantitative assessment of Crohn's perianal fistula complexity and treatment response.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Classify fistula type (Parks' classification); identify internal opening; map primary tract and secondary extensions; detect collections (abscess cavities); assess sphincter integrity; monitor treatment response (particularly Crohn's fistulae after biologic therapy); guide surgical planning
diagnostic_tests.key_findings: T2 hyperintense (bright) tract through sphincter complex; location of internal opening at dentate line level; secondary tracts; supralevator extension; horseshoe configuration; associated collections (T2 bright with rim enhancement on Gd)
diagnostic_tests.indication: ALL complex fistulae before surgery; Crohn's perianal fistulae; recurrent fistulae after failed previous treatment; any fistula where the anatomy is unclear; when anorectal examination is insufficient to determine sphincter involvement
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Does not provide real-time dynamic information; MRI may not replace EUA — they are complementary (MRI for anatomy; EUA for treatment)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Examination Under Anaesthesia (EUA) — Essential for Treatment
diagnostic_tests.description: The definitive investigation AND treatment modality for anal fistula — the gold standard for identifying the internal opening, probing the tract, assessing sphincter involvement, and performing definitive or staged treatment in the same sitting. Performed under general or spinal anaesthesia. Instruments: fistula probe (malleable silver probe); proctoscope; hydrogen peroxide or methylene blue injection (to trace the tract); Parks' retractors.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify internal opening definitively; probe the tract (determine course and sphincter relationship); place seton; perform fistulotomy (simple low fistulae); take biopsies; drain any associated abscess; combined diagnostic + therapeutic
diagnostic_tests.internal_opening_identification: Hydrogen peroxide (3mL) injected via external opening: bubbles appear at the internal opening through the proctoscope. Methylene blue (1mL): blue dye traced to internal opening. Digital palpation for induration at the dentate line. Fistula probe passed from external opening.
diagnostic_tests.probe_caution: NEVER force a fistula probe — forced probing creates FALSE TRACTS, worsens the fistula, and provides wrong information. The probe follows the path of least resistance.

diagnostic_tests.description: High-frequency rotating endoanal ultrasound probe provides real-time circumferential imaging of the sphincter complex and perisphincterc tissues. 3D endoanal ultrasound with hydrogen peroxide injection (H2O2-enhanced EAUS) is highly accurate for identifying the internal opening and fistula tract course. Particularly useful for: assessment of sphincter integrity before surgery (identifying pre-existing sphincter defects that would increase incontinence risk); and in centres without readily available MRI.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Map fistula tract; identify internal opening; assess sphincter integrity; identify horseshoe extensions
diagnostic_tests.comparison_with_mri: EAUS accuracy comparable to MRI for intersphincteric and low transsphincteric fistulae; MRI superior for suprasphincteric and extrasphincteric fistulae and for supralevator extensions; EAUS is faster and less expensive; MRI provides better soft tissue context
diagnostic_tests.h2o2_enhancement: Injection of hydrogen peroxide (1-2mL) into the external opening produces echogenic bubbles that trace the fistula tract in real-time on ultrasound — significantly increases sensitivity for identifying internal opening and tract course

diagnostic_tests.description: Water-soluble contrast injection into the external opening, followed by plain X-ray or fluoroscopy to trace the fistula tract. Largely SUPERSEDED by MRI and EAUS in modern practice — poor accuracy (<40% for accurately identifying the internal opening and sphincter involvement). Occasionally used for: enterocutaneous fistulae (to confirm connection to bowel and assess tract length, which guides spontaneous closure potential); when MRI is contraindicated; some complex post-surgical fistulae.
diagnostic_tests.current_use: Mainly for enterocutaneous fistulae (not anal fistulae); largely replaced by MRI for perianal fistulae
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Low accuracy for internal opening identification; does not show sphincter relationship well; contrast may not fill complete tract

diagnostic_tests.description: Mandatory in all patients with suspected or known Crohn's disease presenting with perianal fistula. Also indicated in: patients with perianal fistula and concurrent diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, weight loss, or abdominal symptoms; patients with multiple or recurrent perianal fistulae without clear cryptoglandular cause; when rectal mucosal assessment is needed before fistula surgery (proctitis on colonoscopy contraindicates fistulotomy).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose or assess Crohn's disease activity (guide biologic treatment); assess rectal mucosa (proctitis — contraindicates fistulotomy); exclude colorectal malignancy; assess disease extent in IBD
diagnostic_tests.key_finding: Crohn's proctitis on colonoscopy: contraindicates any form of sphincter division — seton drainage only until proctitis controlled; biologic therapy required

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Biopsy of Fistula Tract / External Opening
diagnostic_tests.description: Tissue biopsy from the fistula tract or granulation tissue at the external or internal opening. Indicated when: atypical appearance; multiple fistulae; long-standing non-healing despite treatment; suspicion of Crohn's (granulomas); suspicion of TB (caseating granulomas, AFB); patient from TB-endemic area (India); elderly patient with risk of anal SCC; change in character of chronic fistula (suggests malignant transformation).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude malignancy (anal SCC); confirm Crohn's (non-caseating granulomas); diagnose TB (caseating granulomas, AFB ZN stain, TB culture); identify unusual organisms
diagnostic_tests.india_note: TB culture and AFB smear should be sent routinely in India for all biopsies from complex perianal fistulae without clear cryptoglandular cause

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool Culture, Fistula Swab Culture, and Pus Culture
diagnostic_tests.description: Microbiological culture of discharge from the fistula or pus from associated abscess identifies causative organisms and guides antibiotic therapy — particularly important for: TB fistulae (Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture — takes 6-8 weeks; send to specialist TB laboratory); Crohn's fistulae with superinfection; HIV-positive patients (unusual organisms including CMV, Cryptosporidium); patients not responding to standard treatment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify causative organisms; detect TB; guide antibiotic therapy; identify resistant organisms (MRSA)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT Scan Pelvis and Abdomen (CT Fistulogram)
diagnostic_tests.description: CT with oral, IV, and rectal contrast provides overview of pelvic anatomy and can demonstrate supralevator collections, pelvic extensions, fistula connection to hollow organs (bladder, vagina), and associated intra-abdominal pathology. CT fistulogram (contrast injected into external fistula opening with CT imaging) is useful for enterocutaneous fistulae — demonstrates the intestinal connection.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess complex supralevator collections; demonstrate fistula connection to bladder or vagina (colovesical, rectovaginal); assess intestinal disease in Crohn's; CT fistulogram for enterocutaneous fistulae
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Inferior to MRI for sphincter anatomy and local fistula tract details

diagnostic_tests.description: Measurement of anal resting and squeeze pressures. Important pre-operatively to establish a baseline continence profile — particularly in: women with prior obstetric injury (may have subclinical sphincter damage); elderly patients; patients with previous anorectal surgery; any patient with pre-existing bowel control difficulties. Low pre-operative resting or squeeze pressure significantly increases incontinence risk after any form of sphincter division.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Pre-operative continence baseline; risk assessment for sphincter-dividing procedures; guide treatment choice

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Inflammatory Markers (CRP, ESR, FBC) and Crohn's Assessment (Faecal Calprotectin)
diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated CRP and ESR in a patient with complex perianal fistula suggests active IBD or systemic sepsis. Faecal calprotectin >200 µg/g suggests active intestinal inflammation (Crohn's or UC). Full blood count: anaemia (Crohn's, sepsis); eosinophilia (parasitic infection); thrombocytosis (chronic inflammation).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess systemic inflammation; screen for Crohn's disease activity; guide biologic treatment initiation

medicines.note: Anal fistula treatment is primarily SURGICAL — most fistulae cannot be resolved with medications alone. However, medications play critical roles in: managing infection and inflammation; treating associated Crohn's disease with biologics; preparing for surgery; maintaining remission after Crohn's fistula treatment; and managing symptoms while awaiting or between procedures. All medications and surgical treatments require specialist colorectal surgery and/or gastroenterology involvement.

treatment_philosophy.simple_low: Simple low intersphincteric or low transsphincteric fistula: PRIMARY FISTULOTOMY (laying open) — single-stage surgery; excellent cure rate (>90%); day case; minimal morbidity
treatment_philosophy.complex_high: Complex or high fistulae: STAGED APPROACHES — start with draining seton to control sepsis; plan definitive sphincter-sparing surgery; biologics for Crohn's; multidisciplinary team management
treatment_philosophy.crohns: Crohn's fistulae: COMBINED medical + surgical — biologic therapy (anti-TNF) + seton drainage; treat active luminal disease; avoid fistulotomy in active proctitis

categories.category_name: Antibiotics — For Perianal Sepsis and Crohn's Fistula
categories.purpose: Control acute sepsis associated with fistula; reduce inflammation to facilitate healing; used as adjuncts in Crohn's perianal fistula (not curative but reduce sepsis and inflammation, allowing biologic treatment to work).

medicines.name: Metronidazole
medicines.dosage: 400mg three times daily orally; 500mg IV TDS (hospitalised sepsis); 400mg TDS for Crohn's perianal fistula — courses of 4-12 weeks
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE antibiotic for perianal sepsis (anaerobic cover — perianal organisms are predominantly anaerobes); Crohn's perianal fistula (reduces perianal inflammation and improves fistula drainage — used ALONGSIDE biologic therapy, not as sole treatment); maintenance therapy in Crohn's awaiting biologic response
medicines.mechanism: Nitroimidazole — enters anaerobic bacteria and is reduced to a reactive form that damages bacterial DNA; active against Bacteroides, Clostridium, Fusobacterium (dominant perianal flora)
side_effects: Peripheral neuropathy (prolonged courses >3-4 weeks — monitor; reduce dose if symptoms develop)
Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — STRICT ALCOHOL AVOIDANCE
medicines.note: Metronidazole alone DOES NOT cure fistulae — it reduces sepsis and inflammation; fistulae recur on stopping unless the underlying tract has been surgically or biologically addressed

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin
medicines.dosage: 500mg twice daily orally; 400mg IV BD (severe sepsis); typically combined with metronidazole for perianal fistula — 4-12 week courses
medicines.use_case: Combined with metronidazole for perianal sepsis (gram-negative aerobic cover — E. coli, Klebsiella); Crohn's perianal fistula (the metronidazole + ciprofloxacin combination is the standard antibiotic regimen — used for 12-16 weeks in Crohn's fistula as a bridge to biologic therapy)
medicines.mechanism: Fluoroquinolone — inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal against gram-negative enteric bacteria
side_effects: Tendinopathy (QT prolongation risk — ECG if prolonged)
medicines.crohns_fistula_evidence: ACCENT-II substudy and multiple RCTs: metronidazole + ciprofloxacin for 12 weeks reduces perianal drainage in Crohn's fistulae by 40-50%; used as bridge to infliximab; combining antibiotics with infliximab achieves better early response than infliximab alone

medicines.name: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Co-amoxiclav)
medicines.use_case: Acute perianal abscess with cellulitis; post-operative wound infection; where metronidazole + ciprofloxacin cannot be used; broad-spectrum cover for mixed perianal flora

categories.category_name: Biological Therapy for Crohn's Perianal Fistula
categories.purpose: Anti-TNF biologics are the CORNERSTONE of treatment for Crohn's perianal fistulae — the most evidence-based pharmacological treatment available. They reduce fistula output, induce complete fistula closure, maintain remission, and prevent recurrence when combined with surgical seton drainage. Used in combination with antibiotics and surgical seton.
categories.note: ALL Crohn's perianal fistulae with complexity should be discussed in a multidisciplinary team (MDT) including a gastroenterologist and colorectal surgeon before initiating biologic therapy. TB screening (TB IGRA/Mantoux) and hepatitis B screen are MANDATORY before starting any biologic.

medicines.name: Infliximab (Anti-TNF-alpha Monoclonal Antibody)
medicines.dosage: Induction: 5mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, and 6; Maintenance: 5mg/kg IV every 8 weeks; dose may be escalated to 10mg/kg or interval shortened (every 4-6 weeks) for loss of response
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE biologic for Crohn's perianal fistulae; complex perianal Crohn's fistulae not responding to antibiotics and surgical seton drainage; active luminal Crohn's with perianal fistula; fistula maintenance therapy
medicines.mechanism: Chimeric (mouse-human) IgG1 monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha — neutralises both soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha; reduces T-cell and macrophage-driven transmural Crohn's inflammation; promotes fistula tract fibrosis and closure
medicines.pivotal_evidence: ACCENT-II trial (Sands BE et al., NEJM 2004): infliximab maintenance (every 8 weeks) achieved complete fistula closure in 36% vs 19% placebo at 54 weeks; reduced number of draining fistulae; reduced perianal disease activity
side_effects: Infusion reactions (acute: fever, chills, hypotension during infusion; delayed: serum sickness-like reaction 1-14 days post-infusion)
Serious infections — increased risk of bacterial, viral (reactivation of TB, HBV, Herpes Zoster), and fungal infections; screen for latent TB before starting (IGRA test)
Lymphoma (small increased risk with long-term anti-TNF + thiopurine combination — TNF-alpha inhibition alone carries very low cancer risk)
Demyelinating disease (rare — avoid in multiple sclerosis)
Cardiac failure worsening (avoid in NYHA III-IV heart failure)
medicines.screening_before_starting: TB IGRA (Quantiferon Gold) — treat latent TB if positive BEFORE starting; HBV serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc) — prophylactic antiviral if HBV exposure; CXR; blood counts; LFTs; pregnancy test
medicines.monitoring: CRP (treatment response); faecal calprotectin; drug level monitoring (infliximab trough levels); anti-infliximab antibody levels (to detect immunogenicity/loss of response)

medicines.name: Adalimumab (Anti-TNF-alpha — Subcutaneous)
medicines.dosage: Induction: 160mg at week 0, then 80mg at week 2; Maintenance: 40mg every 2 weeks (can increase to 40mg weekly for loss of response)
medicines.use_case: Crohn's perianal fistulae — FIRST-LINE biologic alternative to infliximab (subcutaneous — patient self-administered at home; no IV infusion centre required); patients who lose response to or are intolerant of infliximab
medicines.mechanism: Fully human IgG1 monoclonal anti-TNF antibody — same mechanism as infliximab; fully human = lower immunogenicity; subcutaneous administration
medicines.pivotal_evidence: CHARM trial: adalimumab maintenance therapy significantly reduced fistula output and improved complete fistula closure vs placebo in Crohn's patients with perianal fistulae
medicines.advantage: Subcutaneous self-injection at home; no infusion centre; lower immunogenicity than infliximab (fully human); may be effective after infliximab failure (second anti-TNF)
medicines.side_effects: Similar to infliximab; injection site reactions (more common with subcutaneous); same infection and lymphoma considerations

medicines.name: Vedolizumab (Anti-Integrin — Gut-Selective)
medicines.dosage: 300mg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6; then every 8 weeks
medicines.use_case: Crohn's perianal fistulae in patients who have failed anti-TNF therapy; patients with contraindications to anti-TNF (TB, malignancy history, demyelinating disease, heart failure); GEMINI long-term data shows modest but significant benefit for perianal fistulae
medicines.mechanism: Humanised monoclonal antibody against α4β7 integrin — blocks gut-specific lymphocyte homing to intestinal mucosa; gut-selective (does NOT affect systemic immunity as broadly as anti-TNF → lower infection risk)
medicines.advantage: Gut-selective → lower systemic infection risk; better for patients who have serious infections on anti-TNF; do not need TB screening (gut-selective)
medicines.note: Slower onset of action than infliximab — may take 6-12 months for full perianal fistula response

medicines.name: Ustekinumab (Anti-IL-12/23)
medicines.dosage: Induction: weight-based single IV dose (260mg for <55kg; 390mg for 55-85kg; 520mg for >85kg); Maintenance: 90mg SC every 8 weeks or 12 weeks
medicines.use_case: Crohn's perianal fistulae — third-line after anti-TNF failure; UNIFI extension data shows perianal fistula healing benefit; increasingly used as second-line before vedolizumab due to faster onset
medicines.mechanism: Fully human antibody against IL-12 and IL-23 (p40 subunit) — inhibits Th1 and Th17 inflammatory pathways central to Crohn's transmural inflammation and fistula formation
medicines.advantage: Good safety profile; no TB screening required (different mechanism); effective across many Crohn's manifestations

medicines.name: Darvadstrocel (Alofisel) — Allogeneic Adipose-Derived Stem Cells
medicines.form: Local injection into fistula tract (suspension for injection)
medicines.dosage: 120 million cells injected directly into the fistula tract (internal and external openings) in a single session after surgical preparation of the tract (debridement + curettage + closure of internal opening)
medicines.use_case: BREAKTHROUGH TREATMENT: Complex perianal Crohn's fistulae refractory to conventional therapy AND at least one anti-TNF agent; EMA-approved (2018) specifically for this indication; provides a non-surgical, sphincter-preserving option for very complex refractory Crohn's fistulae
medicines.mechanism: Adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells injected directly into the fistula tract; exert local immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory effects; promote healing through growth factor secretion (HGF, TGF-beta, VEGF); promote tissue regeneration and fistula closure
medicines.pivotal_evidence: ADMIRE-CD trial (Panés J et al., Lancet 2016): combined remission (fistula closure + no abscess) achieved in 50% Alofisel vs 34% placebo at 24 weeks; durable response at 52 weeks
medicines.availability: EMA-approved in Europe; limited availability in India and many countries; expensive; specialist centres only

categories.category_name: Surgical Treatments — Core Interventions for Anal Fistula
categories.purpose: Surgery is the definitive treatment for anal fistula in the majority of cases. The choice of surgical procedure is the most critical decision in fistula management — determined by fistula complexity, sphincter involvement, pre-existing continence, and associated conditions.

medicines.name: Fistulotomy (Laying Open)
medicines.description: The GOLD STANDARD treatment for simple low anal fistulae. The entire fistula tract is laid open — a probe is passed from the external to the internal opening, and all tissue overlying the probe is divided. The resulting wound heals by secondary intention (granulation) over 4-8 weeks. ONLY SAFE for: intersphincteric fistulae (no sphincter at risk); low transsphincteric fistulae where the amount of external sphincter involved is acceptable (<30% of total EAS length in most patients).
medicines.use_case: Simple intersphincteric fistula; low transsphincteric fistula with minimal sphincter involvement; superficial subcutaneous fistula
medicines.continence_risk: Very low for intersphincteric fistulae (<5% minor incontinence); moderate for low transsphincteric (5-15% risk of gas/minor soiling depending on extent of sphincter divided)
side_effects: Incontinence (primary risk — related to amount of sphincter divided)
Delayed wound healing (4-8 weeks — wound heals by secondary intention)

medicines.name: Seton Placement (Cutting Seton or Draining/Loose Seton)
medicines.description: A seton is a thread, suture, or silastic loop passed through the fistula tract. TWO TYPES: (1) DRAINING (LOOSE) SETON: a non-cutting loop loosely placed to allow drainage of the tract, prevent abscess formation, and stimulate fibrous reaction — used as a LONG-TERM DRAINAGE device in complex fistulae while awaiting definitive treatment or as palliation; (2) CUTTING (STAGED) SETON: a tight thread progressively tightened (at monthly intervals) causing slow gradual division of the sphincter with concurrent fibrous reaction — the sphincter heals as it is divided, theoretically preserving continence. CUTTING SETON has higher incontinence risk than previously thought — largely replaced by sphincter-preserving procedures (LIFT, flap) for most complex fistulae.
medicines.draining_seton_uses: Complex fistulae awaiting biologic treatment response (Crohn's); control of acute sepsis; horseshoe fistulae (limb drainage); long-term palliation if definitive surgery declined or too risky; pre-biologic drainage (seton drainage improves biologic response in Crohn's perianal fistula)
medicines.cutting_seton_uses: Occasionally used for transsphincteric fistulae when other sphincter-sparing options unavailable; fallen out of favour due to significant incontinence risk
side_effects: Incontinence (cutting seton — 15-50% rates of some incontinence)

medicines.name: LIFT Procedure (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract)
medicines.description: A sphincter-preserving procedure — access is gained through the intersphincteric plane; the fistula tract is identified, ligated, and divided in the intersphincteric space (between the IAS and EAS); the wound is then closed. The sphincter is NOT divided. Initially described by Rojanasakul in 2007; excellent results in many centres for transsphincteric fistulae. Variation: BioLIFT (LIFT with bioprosthetic plug reinforcement of the intersphincteric space).
medicines.use_case: Transsphincteric anal fistulae (low to moderate complexity) as a sphincter-preserving alternative to fistulotomy; particularly in patients at higher incontinence risk (women, prior obstetric injury, elderly)
medicines.healing_rate: 57-80% healing in various series; higher in experienced hands; recurrence rate 14-30%
medicines.continence_risk: Very low — no sphincter division; minimal incontinence risk
medicines.advantage: Sphincter-preserved; repeatable if recurs; good option between seton and advancement flap

medicines.name: Mucosal Advancement Flap (Rectal Advancement Flap)
medicines.description: A sphincter-preserving technique — after curettage of the fistula tract, a flap of mucosa, submucosa, and internal sphincter is raised from the rectum and advanced to cover the internal opening (the source of fistula contamination). By closing the internal opening with healthy tissue (without sphincter division), the fistula tract can heal. The external opening is left open to drain.
medicines.use_case: Complex transsphincteric fistulae where fistulotomy would risk incontinence; high fistulae; anterior fistulae in women; recurrent fistulae after LIFT failure; Crohn's fistulae (in remission, no active proctitis)
medicines.healing_rate: 60-75% in acute cases; lower in Crohn's (40-55%); success depends on no active proctitis
medicines.continence_risk: 5-15% minor incontinence (from manipulation of internal sphincter in flap elevation)
medicines.contraindication: Active Crohn's proctitis (impaired healing); active abscess at the time of repair

medicines.name: VAAFT (Video-Assisted Anal Fistula Treatment)
medicines.description: A minimally invasive sphincter-preserving technique using a specially designed fistuloscope (rigid 8Fr endoscope) passed through the external opening to visualise the fistula tract, identify the internal opening from within, and ablate the tract from the inside using electrocautery. The internal opening is then closed with a stapler, sutures, or flap. Allows direct visualisation of the entire tract including secondary extensions.
medicines.use_case: Complex and recurrent anal fistulae; horseshoe fistulae; any fistula where complete tract visualisation is desired before treatment; minimally invasive option
medicines.advantage: Minimally invasive; sphincter-sparing; direct tract visualisation; secondary extensions identified and ablated; suitable for complex tracts

medicines.name: Fibrin Glue Injection
medicines.description: Biological fibrin sealant (prepared from pooled donor plasma — containing fibrinogen, thrombin, calcium chloride) injected into the fistula tract (from external opening with simultaneous closure of internal opening) creates a fibrin plug that fills and seals the tract while stimulating fibroblast ingrowth and healing.
medicines.use_case: Low-complexity fistulae; adjunct to other procedures; patients unfit for surgery; bridge treatment; historically popular — declining in use due to modest long-term results
medicines.healing_rate: 14-63% (highly variable); better results in shorter (<2cm) simple tracts; worse in complex and Crohn's fistulae
medicines.advantage: Non-surgical; safe; no sphincter risk; can be repeated
medicines.limitation: Lower long-term healing rates than other techniques; expensive; requires preparation

medicines.name: Anal Fistula Plug (AFP) — Bioprosthetic Plug
medicines.description: A cone-shaped bioprosthetic plug (typically made from lyophilised porcine small intestinal submucosa — SIS) inserted into the fistula tract from the internal opening outward. The plug acts as a scaffold for tissue ingrowth and the internal opening is secured with sutures. Provides a biologic matrix for healing without sphincter division.
medicines.use_case: Transsphincteric and high complex fistulae as a sphincter-preserving option; patients preferring a single-stage procedure; moderate evidence base
medicines.healing_rate: 14-80% (very variable); higher early series not replicated in larger trials; average ~50% long-term
medicines.advantage: Simple insertion; no sphincter risk; can be performed under local anaesthesia in some settings
medicines.limitation: Plug extrusion is the primary failure mode (plug falls out before incorporation); expensive; variable results

categories.purpose: Supporting healing, managing discharge, and preventing secondary infection.

medicines.name: Wound Packing and Irrigation — Warm Saline
medicines.dosage: Wash the external opening with warm saline or plain warm water twice daily; gentle irrigation with a syringe if accessible; dry with soft gauze pat; apply a small gauze pad to absorb discharge
medicines.use_case: ALL anal fistula patients — maintaining cleanliness of the external opening reduces secondary bacterial contamination, reduces pruritus, and reduces perianal skin excoriation

medicines.name: Barrier Cream — Zinc Oxide Paste
medicines.dosage: Apply a thin layer to the perianal skin around (not into) the fistula external opening after cleaning; acts as moisture barrier
medicines.use_case: Protect perianal skin from chronic discharge-related excoriation and chemical dermatitis; reduce pruritus ani
medicines.mechanism: Physical barrier preventing faecal and discharge contact with perianal skin; mild antibacterial; zinc promotes wound healing

medicines.name: Stool Softeners (Lactulose, Macrogol, Isabgol)
medicines.dosage: As per individual product instructions; target Bristol Type 4 soft stools
medicines.use_case: Essential for ALL fistula patients — soft stools reduce intraluminal pressure in the anal canal; reduce straining (which increases risk of spreading infection); facilitate postoperative healing; prevent post-operative constipation-related wound dehiscence
medicines.note: Particularly important post-operatively — hard stools can disrupt fistulotomy wounds and prevent healing

diet_and_nutrition.overview: While diet does not directly cause or cure anal fistula (unlike anal fissure where constipation is a direct cause), dietary optimisation plays a critical supporting role in: facilitating healing of fistula wounds post-surgery; reducing constipation and straining (which increase intraluminal anal pressure and may worsen fistula drainage or post-operative wound problems); supporting immune function (particularly important for Crohn's and TB fistulae); and maintaining nutritional status in complex fistulae with significant output.

recommended_foods.category: High-Fibre Diet for Stool Consistency Optimisation
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — soft stools reduce straining and intraluminal anal pressure; prevent post-operative wound complications; maintain overall anorectal health

items.food: Whole grains (ragi, jowar, bajra, whole wheat atta, brown rice), Legumes (dal, chana, rajma), Vegetables, Fruits
items.benefit: Maintains soft, well-formed stools (Bristol Type 4); reduces straining during defecation; prevents constipation that would stress fistula wound sites post-operatively; general anorectal health
items.frequency: Daily — maintain the same high-fibre diet as for anal fissure; target 25-35g fibre/day

items.benefit: Stool softening and bulking; reduces straining; most practical and affordable fibre supplement; particularly important post-operatively
items.frequency: 1-2 teaspoons in 300mL water once or twice daily; continue long-term

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — protein is essential for: surgical wound healing; immune function (particularly against perianal infection); muscle maintenance (prevents cachexia in complex fistulae); collagen synthesis for fistula tract fibrosis

items.food: Eggs, Chicken, Fish, Mutton (lean), Dal and legumes (combined plant protein), Paneer, Curd
items.benefit: Adequate protein (1.2-1.5g/kg/day for post-surgical healing) accelerates wound healing; supports immune function; essential amino acids for collagen and tissue synthesis
items.frequency: Every meal — ensure protein source at breakfast, lunch, and dinner

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (Mediterranean diet) reduce systemic and local gut inflammation; may improve Crohn's disease activity (adjunctive to biologic therapy)

items.food: Oily fish (omega-3), Turmeric (curcumin), Ginger, Olive oil, Berries, Green tea, Leafy vegetables
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory (reduces TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1β); complementary to biologic therapy in Crohn's fistula; supports mucosal healing; antioxidant protection

In Crohn's disease, EEN (consuming a complete liquid nutritional formula as the sole diet for 6-8 weeks) induces remission in 50-80% of active Crohn's disease — comparable to corticosteroids but without steroid side effects; reduces gut inflammation; allows perianal fistula improvement; widely recommended in paediatric Crohn's and increasingly used in adult Crohn's flares
items.frequency: Under dietitian supervision — 6-8 week course in active Crohn's flare
items.india_note: Commercial elemental and polymeric formulas: Ensure, Fortisip, Nutrison, Ensure Plus; enteral feeding via NG tube if oral tolerance inadequate

recommended_foods.category: Zinc, Vitamin C, and Vitamin D — Wound Healing Micronutrients

items.food: Zinc sources: Pumpkin seeds, Sesame (til), Legumes, Meat, Eggs, Dairy; Vitamin C: Amla, Guava, Lime; Vitamin D: Oily fish, Eggs, Sunlight
items.benefit: Zinc: essential for wound healing, immune function (neutrophil and lymphocyte activity), and collagen synthesis; deficiency common in IBD and malnutrition. Vitamin C: cofactor for collagen synthesis (required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen); antioxidant; immune support. Vitamin D: immune modulation; Vitamin D deficiency common in Crohn's disease

recommended_foods.evidence: Critical — high-output enterocutaneous fistulae cause massive fluid, electrolyte, protein, and micronutrient losses; malnutrition is the single most important reversible factor preventing spontaneous fistula closure

items.food: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) or Total Enteral Nutrition (TEN) — Medical
items.benefit: In high-output enterocutaneous fistulae: bowel rest (TPN) or post-fistula enteral feeding (TEN) may allow spontaneous fistula closure; maintains nutritional status; allows surgical correction when the patient is optimised; TPN gives bowel rest reducing fistula output; TEN (distal to the fistula) provides nutrition with reduced fistula output
items.protocol: SNAP protocol for enterocutaneous fistulae: Sepsis control; Nutrition (TPN or EN); Anatomy delineation (CT fistulogram); Protect skin; Definitive surgical plan
items.note: TPN/TEN in enterocutaneous fistula is a medical inpatient management — requires specialist nutritional support team

foods_to_avoid.food: Highly spicy foods during active infection and post-operatively
foods_to_avoid.reason: Capsaicin passed in stool irritates inflamed perianal wound and fistula opening; worsens post-defecation burning at the wound site; avoid during active fistula treatment and post-operative period

foods_to_avoid.food: Alcohol (during antibiotic treatment and biologic therapy)
foods_to_avoid.reason: ABSOLUTE during metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction); alcohol reduces immune function and impairs wound healing; avoid during biologic therapy (reduces resistance to infections); avoid during post-operative recovery

foods_to_avoid.food: Constipating foods (refined grains, excess dairy, insufficient fibre) — particularly post-operatively
foods_to_avoid.reason: Constipation and hard stools post-operatively can disrupt healing wounds; increase straining-related wound stress; avoid refined white rice, white bread, maida, and insufficient fluid intake

foods_to_avoid.food: High-residue foods (particularly after fistulotomy wound healing phase)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Very high-residue foods (corn husks, raw vegetables with intact fibres) may physically irritate fresh fistulotomy wounds; generally soft cooked fibres are better tolerated in the first 2-4 weeks post-operatively

sample_meal_plan.note: Post-fistula surgery (fistulotomy or seton) meal plan supporting wound healing, soft stools, and immune nutrition.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Warm water (2 glasses) + 1 teaspoon Isabgol in water
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Soft ragi or whole wheat porridge (dalia) with milk + 1-2 eggs (scrambled or boiled) + 1 glass warm water or coconut water
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1 bowl papaya (gut motility) + 1 small cup curd (probiotics, protein)
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Soft dal (moong or masoor — well cooked) + brown rice or 2 soft chapati + 1 cooked vegetable sabzi (not highly spiced — lauki or tori preferred) + 1 cup curd
sample_meal_plan.afternoon: Guava or pear + warm ginger tea + turmeric milk (for anti-inflammatory support)
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Khichdi (dal + rice — soft, easily digestible) + steamed chicken or fish (protein for healing) + 1 cooked green vegetable
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Warm milk with turmeric + 1 teaspoon Isabgol in water if needed for stool softening

special_dietary_notes: POST-OPERATIVE NUTRITION is especially important — ensure 1.2-1.5g protein/kg/day; adequate zinc and Vitamin C; maintain soft stools with fibre and Isabgol; avoid constipation

CROHN'S FISTULA diet: Mediterranean-type anti-inflammatory diet; Exclusive Enteral Nutrition (EEN) during Crohn's flares; daily Vitamin D supplementation (deficiency common in Crohn's); avoid trigger foods specific to individual patient

TB FISTULA diet: TB is catabolic (causes weight loss and muscle wasting); high-protein, high-calorie diet is essential alongside TB medications; DOTS regime: rifampicin causes orange-red discolouration of urine and tears — reassure patients

fistulotomy_wound_care: Warm sitz baths 2-3 times daily and after every bowel movement — the most important wound care measure; promotes healing, cleans wound, reduces bacterial colonisation
Gentle cleaning of the open wound with warm saline or plain warm water; dry with soft gauze; apply dry non-adherent gauze dressing lightly
Wound packing: in the early post-operative period, the wound may need light gauze packing to prevent premature skin bridge formation — district nursing or daily wound dressing in hospital follow-up
Do NOT use antiseptics (Dettol, Savlon, hydrogen peroxide) directly on the healing wound — cytotoxic to healing tissue; plain warm saline or water is best
Avoid tight underwear or clothing that presses on the wound — loose cotton underwear; avoid synthetic fabrics
Return to work: most patients can return to a desk job in 1-2 weeks post-fistulotomy; physically demanding work 4-6 weeks
seton_care: Clean the seton thread and perianal area daily with warm water; gentle traction on the seton knot to free it from perianal skin
The seton should be non-cutting (loose) and move freely through the fistula — if it feels too tight, contact the surgeon
The seton is a temporary or long-term device — attend all follow-up appointments; the seton will be removed or exchanged at the surgeon's instruction
Light discharge from the seton tract is expected and normal — wear a small gauze pad to protect clothing

hygiene_and_perianal_care: Use a health faucet (lota), bidet, or damp cotton wool for perianal cleansing after defecation — far superior to dry toilet paper for a patient with active fistula discharge
Apply zinc oxide barrier cream (or Sudocrem) to the perianal skin around the external opening to protect it from maceration and chemical dermatitis from chronic discharge
Change pads/gauze frequently — wet pads promote skin breakdown and bacterial colonisation
Loose, breathable cotton underwear — avoids moisture trapping and irritation

smoking_cessation.importance: Smoking is one of the strongest risk factors for Crohn's disease activity — smokers have significantly more active Crohn's disease, more perianal fistulae, and worse outcomes from biologic therapy. Smoking DOUBLES the risk of Crohn's disease and worsens perianal fistula outcomes dramatically. Smoking cessation is among the most important advice for any Crohn's fistula patient.
smoking_cessation.recommendation: Complete cessation; NRT; varenicline; motivational support

managing_crohns_disease: Medication adherence: maintaining biologic therapy (infliximab/adalimumab) adherence is essential — the single most important predictor of fistula closure in Crohn's; missed doses increase antibody formation and loss of response
Stress management: psychological stress is a major trigger for Crohn's flares which worsen perianal fistula; CBT, mindfulness, adequate sleep
Regular colonoscopy surveillance: in long-standing Crohn's fistulae, perianal Crohn's increases colorectal cancer risk — maintain surveillance programme

Multidisciplinary team (MDT): Crohn's perianal fistula is best managed by an IBD MDT including gastroenterologist, colorectal surgeon, IBD nurse, stoma therapist, and (if needed) psychologist and dietitian
psychological_support: Anal fistula causes significant psychological morbidity — chronic discharge, odour, need to wear pads, sexual embarrassment, recurrent surgeries, and fear of incontinence cause: depression, anxiety, sexual dysfunction, social isolation, reduced quality of life
Normalise the psychological burden: acknowledge that this is a difficult, chronic condition; validate the patient's experience
Crohn's-specific support: IBD charities (Crohn's and Colitis UK; The Gut Trust) provide peer support, information, and advice
Sex and relationship counselling: perianal fistula and surgery significantly affect sexual activity; referral for psychosexual counselling if needed
Support for incontinence after surgery: pelvic floor physiotherapy; continence nurse specialist; biofeedback if post-operative sphincter dysfunction

fistula_monitoring_plan.note: Fistula monitoring tracks healing progress, treatment response, and complication detection. Monitoring intervals and investigations depend on the treatment modality and associated conditions.

green_zone.status: Responding Well — Fistula Healing or Controlled
green_zone.criteria_post_surgery: Post-fistulotomy: wound contracting and granulating well; discharge decreasing; pain reducing; no signs of wound infection; stools soft; patient tolerating warm sitz baths and wound care. Post-seton: discharge controlled; no acute abscess formation; awaiting definitive treatment planning. Crohn's fistula on biologic: fistula output decreasing; patient reporting improvement; CRP trending down; MRI (at 6 months) showing reduced T2 signal hyperintensity
green_zone.action: Continue wound care and warm sitz baths post-fistulotomy; continue dietary fibre; attend all follow-up appointments; post-fistulotomy wound check at 2-4 weeks and 6-8 weeks. Crohn's fistula: continue biologic therapy at maintenance dosing; 6-monthly clinical review; annual MRI to assess response; drug level monitoring; colonoscopy as per IBD schedule.

yellow_zone.criteria: Fistulotomy wound not healing at expected rate (>8-10 weeks for simple fistulotomy without significant improvement); persistent high-volume discharge; pain not improving after seton; Crohn's fistula not reducing output after 6 months of biologic therapy; loss of biologic response (increasing fistula output after initial improvement); new secondary tract developing; drug level monitoring shows subtherapeutic infliximab/adalimumab levels
yellow_zone.action: Surgical review: assess wound for bridging or premature skin closure (requires breakdown to allow healing from base); EUA if anatomy unclear; MRI pelvis to reassess tract extent and secondary tracts. Crohn's: check biologic drug levels and anti-drug antibodies; dose escalate or switch biologic if loss of response; rule out superimposed infection (abscess); ensure antibiotic treatment ongoing; consider adding azathioprine to reduce immunogenicity

red_zone.criteria: Fever and systemic sepsis — acute abscess developing in a fistula patient (particularly post-seton); wound breakdown with spreading cellulitis; new severe pain not explained by expected post-operative course; change in nature of chronic fistula discharge (bloody, purulent, faecal-stained in previously minimal discharge) — possible malignant transformation in chronic fistula; unexpected incontinence after surgery; massive increase in discharge suggesting new tract formation
red_zone.action: URGENT surgical review (same day if fever and acute pain — possible acute abscess requiring emergency drainage). If new incontinence post-sphincterotomy: urgent anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound (assess sphincter integrity); continence nurse specialist. If chronic fistula character change: urgent EUA + biopsy to exclude anal SCC. SEPSIS with perianal fistula: IV antibiotics + urgent EUA and drainage

complications.description: The most feared and most important complication of anal fistula surgery — affecting quality of life as severely as the fistula itself if significant. Results from inadvertent division of too much sphincter muscle. Minor incontinence (flatus/mucus soiling): occurs in 10-20% after fistulotomy for transsphincteric fistulae. Major incontinence (liquid or solid stool): 2-5%. Risk factors: female sex (less sphincter reserve); anterior location; prior obstetric sphincter injury; previous anorectal surgery; suprasphincteric or extrasphincteric fistula.
complications.prevention: Pre-operative anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound to assess sphincter reserve; use sphincter-preserving procedures (LIFT, advancement flap, VAAFT) for complex high fistulae; never perform fistulotomy for high transsphincteric or suprasphincteric fistulae
complications.management: Pelvic floor physiotherapy; biofeedback; PTNS (posterior tibial nerve stimulation); injectable sphincter bulking agents (NASHA Dx gel); sacral nerve stimulation; sphincteroplasty (sphincter repair); stoma if catastrophic incontinence

complications.description: Recurrence after apparently successful treatment is one of the most frustrating outcomes of anal fistula management. Recurrence rates: fistulotomy (simple fistula): 2-8%; LIFT procedure: 15-30%; advancement flap: 20-30%; fibrin glue: 30-60%; botulinum toxin (Crohn's): 40-50%. Causes of recurrence: failure to identify or close the internal opening (the primary source of ongoing infection); missed secondary tracts at surgery; inadequate healing from comorbid conditions (Crohn's, diabetes, immunosuppression); re-infection from the same anal gland.
complications.management: Repeat MRI and EUA; identify missed internal opening or secondary tract; reassess for underlying Crohn's or TB; repeat surgery with attention to cause of failure

complications.description: Blockage of the external opening (from granulation tissue or fibrosis) leads to accumulation of discharge in the fistula tract → acute abscess formation. Patients experience: sudden increase in perianal pain; local swelling; fever; systemic sepsis features. This cycling of discharge-and-blockage is a characteristic pattern of untreated or inadequately treated anal fistula.
complications.management: Urgent drainage (examination under local or general anaesthesia); IV antibiotics; ensure adequate drainage of the external opening; fistula tract re-assessment after acute episode resolves

complications.description: A rare but potentially fatal long-term complication — squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can develop in a long-standing chronic anal fistula tract, particularly in: Crohn's disease (chronic inflammation + fistula for >10-20 years); patients with chronic anal fistula associated with HPV; chronic radiation fistulae. The cancer is often missed because it may not change the external appearance dramatically — the key alert is a CHANGE IN THE CHARACTER of the fistula (more pain, bleeding, friable tissue, purulent discharge changing to bloody).
complications.alarm_features: Change in pain character; new bleeding from fistula; hard or friable tissue at fistula opening; systemic symptoms (weight loss, constitutional); fistula not responding to previously effective treatment
complications.management: BIOPSY any chronic non-healing fistula, particularly with changed character; if SCC confirmed — MDT management (oncology, colorectal surgery, radiation oncology); chemoradiotherapy (Nigro/James protocol) is standard first-line for anal SCC; surgery if residual disease
