complications.complication: Perianal Skin Excoriation and Chronic Dermatitis
complications.description: Chronic perianal discharge causes chemical dermatitis and skin breakdown — the skin becomes raw, erythematous, macerated, and intensely pruritic. Secondary fungal infection (Candida) is common in the chronically moist perianal area. This is a significant quality-of-life complication even for patients with otherwise controlled fistula.
complications.management: Meticulous perianal skin care; barrier creams (zinc oxide); moisture-wicking pads; topical antifungal (clotrimazole 1% cream) if fungal infection; low-potency topical corticosteroid (short courses only) for acute dermatitis flare

complications.complication: Sepsis and Life-Threatening Perianal Necrotising Fasciitis (Fournier's Gangrene)
complications.description: A rare but life-threatening complication — inadequately treated perianal abscess-fistula complex in immunocompromised patients (poorly controlled diabetes, HIV, haematological malignancy, chemotherapy) can progress to necrotising fasciitis (Fournier's Gangrene) — a rapidly spreading synergistic bacterial infection of the perineal fascial planes causing tissue necrosis. Characterised by: rapidly spreading perianal swelling and necrosis; crepitus (gas-forming organisms); systemic sepsis; shock.
complications.management: EMERGENCY: immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin + fluconazole); emergency surgical debridement — wide excision of all necrotic tissue; ICU care; hyperbaric oxygen therapy adjunctively; multiple re-debridements until clean; reconstructive surgery after recovery

complications.description: The chronic nature of anal fistula — persistent discharge, odour, embarrassment, recurrent surgeries, fear of incontinence, and pain — causes significant psychological morbidity comparable to other chronic conditions: depression (40%), anxiety (35%), sexual dysfunction (20-40%), relationship difficulties, social isolation, inability to work, reduced quality of life. These consequences are significantly underrecognised and undertreated.
complications.management: Acknowledge and validate psychological burden; refer to clinical psychologist or psychiatrist if depression/anxiety significant; psychosexual counselling for sexual dysfunction; social work support; IBD charities and support groups; occupational therapy for work rehabilitation

key_points: Crohn's perianal fistulae are the most complex and challenging anal fistulae to treat — requiring lifelong combined medical + surgical management

Active RECTAL PROCTITIS on colonoscopy is an absolute contraindication to fistulotomy — the inflamed rectum cannot support a healing wound; any sphincter division will heal poorly; always control rectal disease with biologic therapy before considering surgery

Seton drainage as a BRIDGE to biologic therapy: place a draining seton (non-cutting) first to control sepsis and allow biologic therapy to induce fistula remission; only consider definitive repair once biologic therapy has achieved significant improvement

COMBINATION TREATMENT is superior: infliximab + seton drainage → significantly higher fistula closure rates than either alone; ACCENT-II trial: 46% complete fistula closure with infliximab + seton vs 23% infliximab alone

Defunctioning stoma: a loop ileostomy or colostomy may be required in severe refractory perianal Crohn's to allow healing; faecal diversion reduces fistula output dramatically; gives perianal tissues time to heal; some patients with quality-of-life-impairing perianal Crohn's prefer a permanent stoma over continued perianal disease
Van Assche MRI score: used to assess treatment response in Crohn's perianal fistulae — reassess MRI at 6-12 months of biologic therapy to document objective improvement
Most commonly caused by obstetric trauma (3rd/4th degree perineal tear) — present 1-3 months post-delivery
Clinical diagnosis: passage of flatus or faeces per vagina; vaginitis; recurrent UTIs; malodorous vaginal discharge
Methylene blue test confirms diagnosis: tampon inserted vaginally, methylene blue instilled per rectum — blue staining confirms rectovaginal communication
Timing of surgical repair: repair EARLY obstetric fistulae immediately (within first 24-48 hours) if possible; if missed, wait at least 3-6 months for inflammation to resolve before repair
Crohn's rectovaginal fistula: ALWAYS exclude Crohn's before surgical repair (Crohn's fistulae do not heal with standard surgical repair alone); biologic therapy first

Surgical options: low anovaginal fistula — perineal repair (Parks' repair, with or without graciloplasty); Martius flap (labial fat pad interposition — excellent for obstetric fistulae); mid-vaginal fistula — transabdominal repair; high fistula — combined abdominal-perineal repair
HIV-positive patients with anal fistula require full STI screen (syphilis, HSV, gonorrhoea, Chlamydia/LGV) — opportunistic perianal infections mimic fistula
Biopsy all perianal ulcers in HIV-positive patients — CMV, Kaposi's sarcoma, lymphoma, and SCC must be excluded
Surgical outcomes are generally acceptable with CD4 >200 cells/µL; CD4 <100: healing impaired; favour non-surgical drainage approaches and optimise ART first
ART optimisation is the single most important adjunct to fistula management in HIV — improving CD4 count dramatically improves wound healing and infection control

Anal SCC has a 40-fold higher incidence in HIV-positive MSM than the general population — any non-healing perianal ulcer or fistula must be biopsied; HPV vaccination recommended for all HIV-positive MSM up to age 45
Symptomatic anal fistula in pregnancy: manage conservatively (sitz baths, antibiotics if abscess component, stool softeners); definitive surgery should be deferred until post-partum where possible
If acute abscess requires drainage during pregnancy: simple drainage under local anaesthesia acceptable; avoid extensive dissection
Post-partum: reassess the fistula after delivery; many Crohn's fistulae worsen post-delivery; definitive fistula assessment and treatment typically recommended from 3-6 months post-delivery
Rectovaginal fistula: if identified during delivery — attempt primary repair immediately; if identified post-partum — wait 3-6 months for tissue recovery before repair

Safe antibiotics in pregnancy: amoxicillin-clavulanate (from 2nd trimester); metronidazole (avoid 1st trimester large doses — theoretical concern); safe from 2nd trimester at standard doses; avoid ciprofloxacin (all trimesters)
India has the world's highest TB burden — TB fistulae are significantly more common in India than in high-income countries; maintain a high clinical index of suspicion

Features suggesting TB fistula: multiple fistulae; pale, indurated, undermined edges; relatively painless; associated perianal skin disease; failure to respond to standard treatment; concurrent pulmonary TB; contact with TB patient; X-ray shows pulmonary disease
Diagnosis: biopsy showing caseating granulomas; ZN stain for AFB; TB culture (Lowenstein-Jensen medium — 6-8 weeks); TB IGRA blood test; GeneXpert PCR on tissue (rapid — results in hours)

Treatment: DOTS regime (4-drug initial phase: isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol × 2 months; continuation phase: isoniazid + rifampicin × 4 months — total 6 months) ALONGSIDE surgical fistula management

Surgery for TB fistula: DELAY until TB medications have been given for at least 4-6 weeks and active infection is controlled; standard surgical fistula treatment (fistulotomy for simple; staged approach for complex) following medical TB control; healing much better once TB infection treated

Drug side effects of TB therapy relevant to fistula patients: rifampicin causes drug interactions (reduces biologic drug levels — important if concurrent Crohn's); isoniazid + rifampicin hepatotoxicity (check LFTs monthly); pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia and arthralgia

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: HPV Vaccine (Human Papillomavirus) — Anal Cancer Prevention
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose schedule (<15 years); 3-dose schedule (≥15 years or immunocompromised); catch-up to age 45 for MSM and HIV-positive
vaccinations_recommended.reason: HPV (types 16, 18) is the primary aetiological agent for anal squamous cell carcinoma — the malignancy that can develop in chronic anal fistulae. HPV also causes anal condylomata (warts) that can obstruct fistula openings and complicate treatment. In MSM (men who have sex with men) — who have a 40-fold increased anal SCC risk and are a significant population with anal fistulae — HPV vaccination is strongly recommended up to age 45. Chronic Crohn's perianal fistulae carry small but real SCC risk; HPV vaccination provides additional protection.
vaccinations_recommended.priority_populations: MSM; HIV-positive; Crohn's disease patients with perianal fistulae; all adolescents before sexual debut

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients with Crohn's disease on immunosuppressive therapy (biologics, thiopurines, corticosteroids) are at significantly higher risk of severe influenza — anti-TNF biologics specifically increase influenza severity risk. LIVE attenuated influenza vaccine (FluMist) is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients — use INACTIVATED influenza vaccine only. Influenza vaccination is strongly recommended annually for all IBD patients on biologic therapy.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV20 or PCV15 + PPSV23 for all immunocompromised patients
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients on anti-TNF biologic therapy have significantly increased risk of serious bacterial infections including pneumococcal disease. The risk is highest in patients on combination immunosuppression (anti-TNF + thiopurine + corticosteroid). Pneumococcal vaccination is MANDATORY before starting biologic therapy for Crohn's fistulae. ACPGBI, ECCO, and BSG guidelines all recommend pneumococcal vaccination for IBD patients on immunosuppression.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 3-dose series; check response (anti-HBs titre) after completion
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis B reactivation is a rare but potentially fatal complication of anti-TNF and other immunosuppressive biologic therapy — HBV reactivation mortality can reach 30%. MANDATORY: screen all patients for HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) before starting biologics. If HBV-naive (anti-HBs negative, anti-HBc negative): vaccinate. If prior HBV exposure (anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative): prophylactic antiviral (tenofovir or entecavir) during biologic therapy. If active HBV (HBsAg positive): treat HBV with antiviral before initiating biologic.
vaccinations_recommended.urgency: Must complete vaccination (or at least 1-2 doses) before starting anti-TNF therapy in non-immune patients

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2 doses for VZV-seronegative patients BEFORE starting immunosuppressive therapy (live vaccine — must complete vaccination at least 3-4 weeks before biologic initiation)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Varicella zoster reactivation (shingles/chicken pox) can be severe or disseminated in patients on anti-TNF biologic therapy. Assess VZV immune status before starting biologics: if VZV IgG negative (never had chickenpox or vaccine) — vaccinate BEFORE starting biologics (live vaccine contraindicated once on immunosuppression). If VZV IgG positive: immune — no action required.
vaccinations_recommended.note: LIVE VACCINE — contraindicated once immunosuppressive therapy has started; vaccination must precede biologic initiation by 3-4 weeks

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Crohn's disease patients on biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab) have impaired immune response to COVID-19 infection and to COVID-19 vaccines (lower antibody titres). Annual updated mRNA booster vaccination is strongly recommended — with an additional dose strategy for those on highest immunosuppression. COVID-19 vaccination in IBD does NOT appear to trigger Crohn's flares. mRNA vaccines are SAFE on all current IBD biologic therapies.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Single dose at birth (India Universal Immunisation Programme); international travellers from low-TB countries
vaccinations_recommended.reason: TB is both a cause of anal fistulae in India AND a critical safety screening issue before starting biologic therapy (anti-TNF biologics reactivate latent TB with potentially fatal consequences). BCG vaccination at birth provides 70-80% protection against severe TB (meningitis, miliary TB) but does not fully prevent all TB infection. For Crohn's patients on anti-TNF therapy: TB IGRA or Mantoux test is MANDATORY before starting; if positive, treat latent TB for 3 months before beginning anti-TNF. BCG vaccination does not affect IGRA testing (unlike Mantoux — IGRA is BCG-vaccination-independent).
vaccinations_recommended.critical_note: In India, virtually all patients have received BCG at birth — but latent TB remains possible despite BCG; ALWAYS perform IGRA (not Mantoux) screening before anti-TNF biologic therapy in India

when_to_see_doctor: Persistent or recurrent perianal discharge from any opening on the perianal skin — even if intermittent or minimal; all perianal sinuses and fistulae require surgical assessment
Recurrent perianal abscesses — two or more abscesses in the same perianal region strongly suggest an underlying fistula requiring definitive treatment
Perianal pain with swelling and fever — possible acute abscess-on-fistula requiring urgent drainage
Passage of flatus or stool from the vagina — possible rectovaginal fistula; requires urgent gynaecological and colorectal assessment
Change in the character of a known chronic fistula — increased pain, bleeding, new swelling, hard tissue, or loss of previous effective drainage; possible malignant transformation; biopsy required
Post-partum perianal symptoms — any anal pain, discharge, or incontinence in the weeks to months after vaginal delivery; obstetric fistula assessment
Patients with Crohn's disease developing new perianal symptoms — early specialist (gastroenterology + colorectal surgery) review before sepsis develops; combined medical + surgical management
Patients from TB-endemic areas (India) with multiple or unusual perianal fistulae — TB fistula must be excluded; biopsy and culture required
Any fistula in an HIV-positive patient or patient on immunosuppression — secondary causes must be excluded; biopsies required

Prior to starting immunosuppressive biologic therapy (infliximab, adalimumab, etc.) for Crohn's: colorectal surgeon assessment of perianal fistulae is mandatory — active perianal sepsis must be controlled (seton placed) before starting biologics
Any rectal bleeding associated with perianal fistula in a patient >45 years — anal SCC must be excluded by biopsy and colonoscopy
emergency_signs: Rapidly spreading perianal and perineal swelling with fever, severe pain, and necrotic skin discolouration — possible FOURNIER'S GANGRENE (necrotising fasciitis) — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY — life-threatening; mortality 20-40%; requires emergency surgical debridement
Severe fever (>39°C) with rigors, hypotension, and perianal pain — possible septicaemia from perianal fistula/abscess — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES — IV antibiotics and surgical drainage urgently needed
Inability to pass urine combined with severe perianal swelling and pain — perianal abscess compressing the urethra or acute urinary retention from perineal infection — URGENT emergency assessment

Severe acute perianal pain, swelling, and fever developing in a known Crohn's fistula patient on biologic therapy — possible biologic-immunosuppression-related deep perianal infection — URGENT assessment (immunosuppression may mask systemic signs of serious infection)
Sudden passage of large amounts of faeces or blood from a perianal fistula external opening — possible bowel rupture or fistulae to major bowel; or malignancy with fistulation — URGENT assessment
Perianal swelling with crepitus (crackling sensation on palpation — like bubble wrap under the skin) — gas-producing organisms suggesting necrotising infection — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is an anal fistula and how is it different from an anal abscess?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: An anal abscess is an acute collection of pus around the anus — causing sudden severe throbbing pain, swelling, redness, and fever. An anal fistula is a chronic abnormal tunnel (tract) that forms between the inside of the anal canal and the skin of the perianal area — causing persistent or intermittent discharge from a small opening on the perianal skin. The relationship: a perianal abscess is often the CAUSE of a fistula. When an abscess forms and either drains spontaneously or is surgically drained, the infected track that caused it may persist as a chronic fistula — the source of ongoing infection from an infected anal gland inside the anal canal. Approximately 30-50% of adequately drained anal abscesses develop a fistula. In summary: abscess = acute, painful, no permanent track. Fistula = chronic, persistent discharge, permanent abnormal track.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why is anal fistula so difficult to treat?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Anal fistula is complex for one central reason: the fistula tract passes through or around the anal sphincter muscles — the muscles that control bowel continence (faecal control). Treatment requires eliminating the fistula completely, but doing so without damaging these sphincter muscles is technically challenging. The dilemma: simply 'laying open' (fistulotomy) works very well for simple low fistulae — but for complex fistulae where a significant portion of sphincter is involved, division of the sphincter causes faecal incontinence, which is as debilitating as the fistula itself. Therefore, for complex fistulae, sphincter-preserving techniques must be used (LIFT procedure, advancement flap, VAAFT, seton) — but these carry higher recurrence rates than simple fistulotomy. For Crohn's fistulae, the underlying inflammatory disease must also be controlled, making it a combined medical + surgical problem. This balance between cure and continence preservation is what makes fistula one of the most surgically complex anorectal conditions.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can an anal fistula heal on its own without surgery?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Almost never — this is a crucial distinction from anal fissures (which often heal spontaneously). An anal fistula has a persistent INTERNAL OPENING at an infected anal gland in the anal canal — as long as this source of infection is present, the fistula will continue to discharge. Without surgical or interventional closure of this internal opening, the fistula will not heal. The external drainage tract is lined by the body's own tissue (epithelialised) which actively maintains the tract open. Very occasionally, a superficial sinus (not a true full-thickness fistula) may heal with prolonged antibiotic treatment and wound care — but a confirmed true anal fistula with an identifiable internal opening at the dentate line requires surgical treatment for durable closure.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is a seton and why has my surgeon placed one?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: A seton is a thread, suture, or silastic rubber loop passed through the fistula tract from the external opening to the internal opening. Your surgeon has placed a seton for one of several reasons: (1) TEMPORARY DRAINAGE — the seton acts as a wick, keeping the fistula tract open and allowing continuous controlled drainage, preventing a painful abscess from building up while you await your definitive treatment; (2) STAGING — in complex fistulae, placing a seton first controls the sepsis and inflammation; then, after 6-12 weeks, the definitive repair (LIFT, flap, Botox for Crohn's) is performed with a better chance of success in clean, non-infected tissue; (3) CROHN'S FISTULA — the seton drains the fistula while biologic therapy (infliximab/adalimumab) works to close it from the inside. You will need to care for the seton daily (clean, prevent it getting tangled), attend follow-up appointments, and expect to keep it for weeks to months until the definitive plan is executed.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I have Crohn's disease and a perianal fistula. What is the best treatment?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Crohn's perianal fistulae require a COMBINED medical and surgical approach — neither alone is fully effective. The current best practice: (1) FIRST — ensure no active rectal proctitis (colonoscopy needed); if proctitis present, treat with biologic therapy first before any surgery; (2) SURGICAL SETON DRAINAGE — a loose seton placed to control sepsis and allow safe biologic therapy; (3) ANTI-TNF BIOLOGIC THERAPY — infliximab (IV infusion every 8 weeks) or adalimumab (SC injection fortnightly) is the most evidence-based treatment for Crohn's perianal fistulae; combination with seton drainage gives best results; (4) ANTIBIOTICS — metronidazole + ciprofloxacin for 12-16 weeks as a bridge to biologic response; (5) Once the fistula output has reduced significantly on biologic therapy, the seton can be removed and the fistula may heal completely. If the fistula fails to close after biologic therapy — LIFT procedure, flap repair, or stem cell therapy (Alofisel) are options. Smoking cessation dramatically improves Crohn's outcomes.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I was diagnosed with a fistula in India — could it be tuberculosis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This is a very important question in India. Yes — TB fistulae are significantly more common in India than in Western countries. You should suspect TB as the underlying cause if: you have multiple fistulae; the fistulae are relatively painless (unlike typical cryptoglandular fistulae which are painful); the fistulae have pale, undermined, chronic-looking edges; you have (or have had) pulmonary TB or been in contact with someone with TB; standard fistula surgery has failed to heal the wound; you have constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). Your surgeon will send tissue biopsies during surgery for: TB culture (6-8 weeks but gold standard); ZN stain for AFB; GeneXpert PCR (rapid — 2 hours); histopathology (caseating granulomas). If TB is confirmed, you will receive DOTS (directly observed treatment short course) anti-TB drugs for 6 months AND appropriate fistula surgery once the infection is adequately controlled.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Will I have incontinence after fistula surgery?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The risk of incontinence depends entirely on the TYPE of fistula and the SURGERY performed. Simple low intersphincteric fistula treated with fistulotomy: very low risk — less than 5% minor gas incontinence; solid stool incontinence is extremely rare. Complex high transsphincteric fistula treated with sphincter-preserving LIFT or flap: very low incontinence risk (these procedures are specifically designed to avoid sphincter damage). Staged cutting seton for high fistula: higher risk — 15-30% some incontinence; reason why cutting setons are increasingly avoided in favour of LIFT/flap. The risk is highest in: women (especially with prior obstetric sphincter injury — sometimes the sphincter was already damaged at childbirth and re-examination under anaesthesia shows a pre-existing defect); patients with prior anorectal surgery; elderly. Your surgeon should discuss the specific incontinence risk based on YOUR individual anatomy before any operation — ask specifically, 'What are your estimated rates of incontinence for my type of fistula with the operation you are planning?'

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can anal fistula cause cancer?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Anal fistula itself does not directly cause cancer. HOWEVER, two important connections exist: (1) Long-standing chronic anal fistulae — particularly in Crohn's disease, where the fistula has been present for 10-20+ years — carry a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) developing WITHIN the chronic fistula tract. The warning signs are: a CHANGE in the character of the fistula — new bleeding, increased pain, hard or irregular tissue at the fistula opening. Any change in a previously stable chronic fistula warrants a BIOPSY. (2) HPV (Human Papillomavirus) infection — a sexually transmitted virus — causes both anal fistula-related perianal disease and anal SCC. HPV vaccination (Gardasil) reduces anal SCC risk. The absolute risk of cancer developing in a typical cryptoglandular fistula without Crohn's is very small — this should not cause excessive anxiety, but explains why we biopsy all chronic or atypical fistulae.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between a fistulotomy and a seton? When is each used?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Fistulotomy (laying open): the entire fistula tract is divided open at once in a single operation. The wound heals from the base over 4-8 weeks (secondary intention). BEST FOR: simple, low fistulae (intersphincteric, or low transsphincteric with minimal sphincter involvement). Cure rate >90%. Cannot be used for complex high fistulae because dividing the sphincter causes incontinence. Seton: a thread or rubber loop passed through the fistula tract. TWO TYPES — (1) Draining (loose) seton: a NON-CUTTING loop left in place to allow drainage and control sepsis; used as a temporary bridge while waiting for definitive treatment (especially in Crohn's fistulae awaiting biologic therapy); (2) Cutting (tight) seton: progressively tightened over weeks to slowly divide the sphincter — now largely abandoned because it causes significant incontinence. In practice: most colorectal surgeons will place a draining seton first for complex fistulae to control sepsis, then plan definitive sphincter-preserving surgery (LIFT, flap) once the acute inflammation settles.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the LIFT procedure and when is it recommended?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) is a sphincter-preserving surgical technique for transsphincteric anal fistulae. The surgeon accesses the intersphincteric plane (the space between the two sphincter muscles) through a small radial incision. The fistula tract is identified within this space, tied off (ligated) with sutures, and divided. This eliminates the internal opening WITHOUT dividing any external sphincter muscle — making the risk of incontinence very low. LIFT is recommended for: transsphincteric fistulae where fistulotomy would risk too much sphincter; patients with reduced sphincter reserve (women with prior obstetric injury; elderly); as a primary sphincter-preserving option in low-moderate complexity fistulae. Healing rate: 57-80%. Advantages: simple procedure; repeatable if unsuccessful; very low incontinence risk; good option between a draining seton and a mucosal advancement flap.
